The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
President Trump is returning from his first ever face-to-face joint meeting
with the presidents of China and Russia.
Instead of briefing the public about it right after the talks in Shenzhen,
Trump has opted to wait.
NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben says the president was notably friendly
with his authoritarian counterparts.
Trump referred to Russian President Vladimir Putin as his friend
and said that he and Chinese leader Xi Jinping have a "outstanding personal relationship."
Both of those leaders are accused of human rights abuses.
In a statement after the meeting, the three said they agreed to talk in the future
about curbing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
They also talked about the importance of "immunities of state officials"
and agreed that the International Criminal Court "must not abuse their jurisdiction."
The statement did not mention the wars in Iran or Ukraine.
Trump says that he plans a press conference Friday at noon.
Danielle Kurtzleben, NPR News.
Aid groups have published a 31-page report on President Trump's Gaza peace plan,
and NPR's Eya Betrawi says the report found failings
in how well the ceasefire is holding in access to humanitarian aid.
The report by nine aid groups gave a failing grade
to the implementation of the past year of ceasefire in Gaza.
It noted Israeli attacks have killed more than 1,650 Palestinians during the ceasefire,
and that Israeli forces have expanded their occupation of Gaza's territory.
The report said just 49 UN-coordinated trucks carried aid into Gaza in September,
with only 2 percent carrying medical supplies.
Israel says Hamas is the main obstacle to improving conditions in Gaza
and that it's facilitating aid as needed.
The report by aid groups that include Oxfam and Refugees International
says countries should replace the Israeli approval process
and military inspections of aid convoys with an independent transparent system.
Eya Betrawi, NPR News, Dubai.
An execution in Texas took over an hour as staff struggled to find a vein tonight.
Inmate Reynaldo Dennis moaned repeatedly about pain.
He was convicted of killing a Houston jeweler during a diamond heist.
The execution came amid renewed scrutiny of capital punishment
following Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike in September.
Investor excitement over AI gave a big boost to anthropic stock today,
but as NPR's Scott Horsley reports, the rest of the market was pummeled.
Anthropic shares soared more than 17 percent in their first day of trading.
The record-setting public offering raised more than 81 billion dollars for the AI giant,
and by day's end, the company had a market value of more than 1.7 trillion dollars.
Investors were not so giddy about the rest of the market.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell two and a quarter percent.
Blue chip stocks were also down,
but the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbling more than 1,100 points.
Despite anthropic's early momentum,
some investors worry the AI boom is nearing an end.
They question whether the huge bats being placed on the sector will eventually pay off.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
The FCC has granted permission to state prisons to jam the signals of cell phones
smuggled to inmates.
The technology is already allowed in federal facilities.
Officials say inmates have used contraband cell phones to run drug rings,
coordinate prison riots, and even order acts of violence.
The major law firm Kirkland and Ellis perform nearly 12 million dollars in free legal work
for the Trump administration to avoid being targeted with an executive order,
and PRS Kerry Johnson reports Democrats in Congress are demanding answers from other law firms.
President Trump slapped several law firms with punitive orders when he returned to the White House
because they hired lawyers or represented clients he did not like.
Several big law firms chose to settle with the Trump administration
to stave off those orders and workplace probes.
Kirkland and Ellis recently told House Democrats
it performed nearly 12 million dollars in free legal work for the administration,
though it balked at helping to rename the Kennedy Center or helping Trump with some other pet projects.
Democrats want to know if other big law firms wound up doing that work
and say they'll make the issue a priority for oversight next year.
Kerry Johnson, NPR News.
President Trump says he has posthumously pardoned baseball star Pete Rose
more than two years after his death and after he was reinstated by Major League Baseball.
Rose is baseball's career hits leader,
but he was banned from baseball after an investigator concluded he bet on the Cincinnati Reds
while playing for and managing the team.
He pleaded guilty in 1990 to filing false tax returns.
I'm Rylan Barton.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
